chunks: And with this chain, I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say:
He was asked about commanding the good and forbidding the evil, whether it is obligatory upon the entire nation, so he said: No.

He was asked: Why? He said: It is only upon the strong, obeyed, and knowledgeable person who knows the good from the evil. It is not upon the weak person who cannot find a way to distinguish which is which, saying from the truth to falsehood.
And the proof of that is the Book of Allah, the Mighty, the Glorious, His saying: 'Let there be from among you a nation that invites to good, enforces what is right, and forbids what is wrong.'
This is specific, not general, just as Allah, the Mighty, the Glorious, said: 'And from the people of Moses is a nation that guides by the truth and thereby administers justice.'

And He did not say 'upon the nation of Moses' nor 'upon all his people,' for they at that time were different nations. And 'nation' can mean one person and upwards, just as Allah, the Mighty, the Glorious, said: 'Indeed, Abraham was a nation, obedient to Allah.'
Meaning obedient to Allah, the Mighty, the Glorious. And it is not obligatory upon anyone who knows this during this period of respite if he has no strength, no excuse, and no obedience (to enforce).

Mas'adah said: And I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: He was asked about the hadith that came from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) that 'The best jihad is a word of justice before an unjust Imam.' What is its meaning? He said: This is when he commands it after knowing it, and he is accepted for it in that matter; otherwise, no.

key_terms.أُمَّةٌ: A nation/group (can mean one person or many)

ai.seo_question: Is commanding the good and forbidding the evil obligatory on every Muslim individually?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the obligation of *Amr bil-Ma'ruf* is not universal (*fard 'ayn*) but conditional upon possessing strength, authority, and knowledge, citing Quranic usage of 'a nation' to denote a specific subset rather than the whole. This establishes the principle of *Takhassus* (specificity) in religious duties, distinguishing between the general community and those qualified to enforce divine law, while noting that during periods of truce or weakness, the burden is lifted from those lacking power or means.
